opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that ReAct doesn't really make assumptions about the environment or the task. If you look at earlier approaches to agents, a lot of them were built for a specific domain. In reinforcement learning you design an agent for Atari, or for Go, or for a robotics task, and the action space, the observation space, and the reward are all tailored to that environment. That works well in that setting, but it doesn't transfer.

ReAct's idea is very simple. On top of whatever actions the environment gives you, you add one more kind of action, which is thinking, or reasoning. Thinking is special because it doesn't change the external world. It only changes the agent's own context, its own internal state. But because language models are good at reasoning in language, that one extra action turns out to be extremely powerful. You can plan, reflect on what just happened, decompose a problem, notice you made a mistake, and update your strategy, all inside the same loop where you're taking actions and getting observations.

So the structure is: observe, think, act, observe again. That's very general. It doesn't matter if the action is calling a search API, clicking on a web page, writing code, or talking to a human. As long as the environment can be expressed in language, or turned into tokens, the same loop applies. That's why I see it as more of a general recipe than a specific method.

Another way to put it: reasoning alone, like chain of thought, is powerful, but it's closed. The model can only use what's already in its head, and it can hallucinate without any feedback. Acting alone, without reasoning, is grounded but kind of shallow, because the agent can't really generalize or plan over long horizons. ReAct combines the two, so reasoning helps you act better, and acting gives you new information that grounds your reasoning. That synergy is something humans do all the time. When you cook, you look at what's in the fridge, you think about what you could make, you try something, you taste it, and you adjust. It's not separate phases.

And I think history has kind of validated this. Many of the agent systems people build today, coding agents, research agents, computer-use agents, are, if you squint, some variant of this loop: a language model that alternates between thinking and calling tools, with observations coming back into the context. The details differ, like how you manage memory, how you train the model, whether the reasoning is visible or hidden, but the backbone is very similar.

That said, I don't think it's the end of the story. Being general doesn't mean it's optimal for everything. There are open questions about long-term memory, about how agents learn from experience over time rather than just within one context window, and about how you define good tasks and rewards. But as a basic abstraction for what an agent built on a language model is, I think "reasoning as an action, interleaved with acting in the world" is about as general as you can get.

r001.rationale: It describes ReAct’s idea as “very simple” and says that adding this action makes the approach “extremely powerful,” linking simplicity with effectiveness.

r002.rationale: It contrasts ReAct’s general loop with earlier agents tailored to specific domains and calls ReAct a “general recipe” that applies across different kinds of actions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that ReAct isn't really an architecture in the traditional sense. It's closer to a minimal statement of what an agent is. An agent is something that can think and can act, and that interleaves the two. Thinking means producing language that has no external effect, and acting means producing something that touches the environment and gets an observation back. Once you accept that framing, almost everything else is a special case.

When we wrote the ReAct paper, the field had two separate threads. One was chain-of-thought, where the model reasons but never touches the world, so it hallucinates and can't fix its own errors. The other was action-only agents, things like WebGPT or early game agents, where the model emits actions but has no space to plan, reflect, or recover. Each one was missing half of what humans do. The insight was just to let the model do both in one trajectory, and to let it decide when to do which. Reasoning becomes a kind of internal action. The "thought" is just an action whose only effect is updating your own context.

Why do I think that's the most general approach? Because the action space is open. You can plug in a search engine, a code interpreter, a browser, a robot arm, or another agent, and the loop doesn't change. Compare that to frameworks that hard-code a planner, an executor, a memory module, a verifier. Those work for the tasks they were designed for, but every piece of structure you add is a prior that may be wrong for the next task. ReAct puts almost all of that structure into the language model and the context, which means it scales with the model instead of against it. When the model gets better, the agent gets better for free. A lot of elaborate agent scaffolds from 2023 are already obsolete for exactly that reason.

The other thing I'd say is that it's the natural interface for learning. If you look at what happened with o1, DeepSeek R1, and the reinforcement learning work since then, the thing being trained is essentially a ReAct trajectory. Long reasoning, tool calls, observations, more reasoning. The reason you can do RL on it is that the whole process is just tokens in a sequence, so you can assign reward and backpropagate through it. A modular system with separate components is much harder to train end to end. So ReAct wasn't just a prompting trick. It turned out to be the data format for agentic RL.

I'll be honest about the limits, though. ReAct says nothing about memory beyond the context window, nothing about how to structure very long horizons, and nothing about how to evaluate whether you're making progress. Those are real problems. But I'd argue they should be solved inside this paradigm, by better models and better environments, rather than by bolting modules on the outside. The generality comes from keeping the loop simple and pushing the intelligence into the model.

r001.rationale: The response argues that keeping the loop simple and avoiding extra structure helps the agent scale with model improvements, presenting simplicity as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It says ReAct’s open action space supports many tools and environments, while structured frameworks work for the tasks they were designed for.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that ReAct gives you a very general loop: you reason about the situation, take an action, observe what happens, and then decide what to do next. You don’t have to specify the entire plan before interacting with the world. You can update your understanding as new information comes in.

That matters because, for many real tasks, you can’t know the right sequence of actions in advance. If you’re browsing a website or debugging a program, the next step depends on what you find. Reasoning helps you choose an action, and the result of that action gives you evidence for further reasoning.

And this loop makes relatively few assumptions about the task. An action could be a search, a piece of code, or a request for clarification. You can also put more specialized procedures inside the loop—a planner, for example, or a workflow for a familiar subtask.

So I wouldn’t say it’s always the most efficient architecture. If you know exactly what needs to happen, a fixed workflow can be better. But as a general starting point for an agent that has to handle unfamiliar situations, reasoning and acting in a feedback loop is a very flexible structure.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes a flexible loop that makes few assumptions, but does not clearly connect the architecture’s simplicity to its effectiveness.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the flexible loop for unfamiliar situations with fixed workflows suited to known tasks, conveying broader applicability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that an agent needs to interact with an environment, and ReAct captures a very general loop for doing that: you reason about what to do, take an action, observe the result, and then update your reasoning. You don’t need to solve the whole problem before you start acting, because some of the information you need only becomes available through interaction.

For example, if you’re answering a question using a search engine, the first result might change what you should search for next. If you’re writing code, running a test might reveal that your original understanding was wrong. Reasoning helps guide the action, and the observation helps ground and revise the reasoning.

What makes this general is that you’re not committing to a particular workflow. You can plan, execute, check your work, or revise your plan within the same loop. The actions could be searches, code execution, or interactions with other people. More structured approaches can still be useful, but I see them as adding structure around this basic interaction loop.

That doesn’t mean every action needs a long reasoning trace. Sometimes you should act immediately. The important thing is having the flexibility to decide what to do next based on what you’ve learned, rather than following a sequence fixed in advance.

r001.rationale: The response calls the interaction loop basic, but does not say that the architecture’s simplicity helps it work effectively.

r002.rationale: It says the approach does not commit to a particular workflow and can accommodate searches, code execution, planning, and other interactions.
